opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think we're at a really interesting inflection point. For a long time, "agents" was more of a promise than a reality. There were a lot of cool demos, but when you actually tried to use them for real work, they'd fall apart after a few steps. What's changed with something like Deep Research is that it's one of the first agentic products people actually use day to day and get real value from.

The reason it works, I think, is a combination of things. The task is well-scoped: go out, find information, synthesize it, and come back with a report. It's forgiving, too. If the model takes a slightly suboptimal path through the web, you still end up with something useful, and it's not taking irreversible actions in the world. And critically, the model was trained end to end on this kind of task, so it learned to recover from mistakes, back up when a search goes nowhere, and keep going. That's very different from wiring a general-purpose model into a hand-built chain of prompts and hoping it holds together.

As for usefulness, the way I think about it is that it compresses work that would take a skilled person hours into a few minutes. If you're getting up to speed on a new domain, doing a competitive landscape, or researching a purchase or a medical question, it's remarkably good. It's not perfect. You still have to read critically, and it can be overconfident or lean on weaker sources. But as a first draft of research, it's already better than what a lot of people would produce themselves.

The bigger takeaway for me is what it signals about where things are headed. Deep Research is an early example of a pattern I think we'll see much more of: pick a domain, define what a good outcome looks like, and train the model to accomplish it over long horizons. As that recipe extends to coding, data analysis, and other kinds of knowledge work, the set of things agents can reliably do is going to grow pretty quickly.

r001.rationale: The response says Deep Research is one of the first agentic products people use day to day and get real value from, and describes it as already useful for several research tasks.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think Deep Research is actually a really interesting case study, because it's one of the first agents that a lot of people have used and gotten real value from. If you had asked me a couple of years ago what the first widely useful agent would look like, I'm not sure I would have guessed "a thing that goes off for ten minutes and writes you a report." But it makes a lot of sense in hindsight.

The reason it works, in my view, is that research is a task where the cost of a mistake is pretty low and the value of breadth is pretty high. If the agent reads fifty sources and gets a couple of details slightly wrong, you're still way ahead of where you'd be if you spent an afternoon doing it yourself, because you can verify the parts that matter. Compare that to something like an agent that's booking travel or sending emails on your behalf. There, one bad action is really costly, and the whole thing falls apart if it's right ninety-five percent of the time.

So where I think we are today is that agents are genuinely useful in domains that share those properties: the output is text or code that a human reviews, the task benefits from the model being able to iterate and use tools, and failures are cheap and visible. Coding agents are the other obvious example. The thing people underestimate is how much of the usefulness comes from the harness around the model, not just the model itself. Giving it search, giving it the ability to execute code, letting it run for a long time and check its own work. A lot of the progress in the last year has come from people figuring out that scaffolding.

Where I'd still be cautious is anything where the agent is taking consequential actions in the world without a human in the loop. The reliability just isn't there yet for most of those use cases, and I think that's where you'll see the next wave of work. But as a knowledge worker's tool, something that does the first eighty percent of a research or coding task so you can focus on the last twenty, I think they're already pretty useful, and that's a bigger deal than it sounds.

r001.rationale: The candidate says Deep Research is one of the first agents people have used and gotten real value from, and concludes that such tools are already pretty useful as knowledge-worker tools.

astra-6.text:
I think Deep Research is a good example of where agents are already useful. You can give it a fairly open-ended question, let it work through a bunch of sources, and come back to something that would have taken you a meaningful amount of time to put together yourself. It doesn’t have to be perfect to be valuable, especially when you can inspect the sources and decide whether you agree with the conclusions.

But I’d distinguish that from being ready to delegate an entire job to an agent. With research, you’re usually reviewing the output before acting on it. Once an agent is taking actions on your behalf, mistakes can be more consequential, and reliability becomes a much bigger issue.

So I’m excited about the usefulness today, particularly for tasks where you can give the agent a clear objective and evaluate what comes back. The harder question is how much supervision it needs, and whether the time you save outweighs the time you spend checking its work.

r001.rationale: The response says Deep Research is already useful and describes it as saving meaningful time on open-ended research tasks.

sol-6.1.text:
I think Deep Research is a good example of where agents are already useful. You give it a fairly open-ended question, it goes off and does work that might otherwise take you hours, and you get back something you can evaluate and build on. It doesn’t have to be perfect to save you a lot of time.

The distinction I’d make is between something that’s useful and something you can reliably hand an entire workflow to. If I’m using an agent for research, I can read the output, check the important claims, and decide what to do next. If it’s taking actions on my behalf, the consequences of a mistake can be much greater.

So I’m excited about what’s available today, especially for tasks where you can give the agent room to work and then review the result. But there’s still a lot of work in getting from an impressive demonstration to a system you trust to do the job consistently.

r001.rationale: The response says Deep Research is already useful and describes it saving substantial time on open-ended tasks.
